info.bio:
Bad Brains es una banda musical estadounidense. Aunque han experimentado con varios estilos y fusiones, son especialmente considerados como una de las primeras bandas hardcore, al desarrollar un estilo rápido en contraste con las otras bandas pioneras del punk.

·Inicios 

Los miembros de Bad Brains se conocieron en el suburbio de Washington D.C., District Heights, Maryland.

El guitarrista Gary Miller' alías Dr. Know,' ya había tocado el bajo en varias bandas funk de la zona

scenes.name: Black rock
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: «El funk es blues acelerado» (Clinton). Pese a Chuck Berry, Little Richard o Bo Diddley, el rock se volvió una forma blanca y la invasión británica reforzó el mito, aunque sus grupos venían del blues negro. Hendrix y Sly lo desmontaron a finales de los sesenta, pero la industria resegregó el rock en pocos años, hasta Prince. El blues eléctrico (Muddy Waters, con su «gran caída tras el golpe del tambor») tuvo su revival ante el público blanco. En la Costa Oeste, multirracial y lejos de los problemas del Norte y del Sur, florecieron bandas mestizas (Sly, Tower of Power, Santana): la influencia del rock psicodélico convirtió el funk de un R&B salvaje en algo universal. A mediados de los setenta el black rock se convirtió en funk, porque la radio obligó a quitar los solos de guitarra; solo algunos resistieron («Who Says a Funk Band Can’t Play Rock?!» de Funkadelic, Slave, Mother’s Finest, los Isley) hasta Prince y la Black Rock Coalition de Vernon Reid (1985), y en los noventa Living Colour, Body Count, Bad Brains o Fishbone.

scenes.name: Hardcore
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El punk como «violento, rápido y ruidoso» tarda en conquistar EE UU, pero cuando lo hace el hardcore se convierte durante dos décadas en el idioma nacional de millones de chavales. Misfits y el «scum-rock»; el crossover punk-metal (Suicidal Tendencies, Corrosion Of Conformity, Agnostic Front); Mission Of Burma en Boston. Washington: Bad Brains (reggae, funk y metal diez años por delante), Minor Threat (el «straight-edge») y Rites Of Spring, inventores del emo-core. San Francisco: Dead Kennedys de Jello Biafra, D.R.I. (thrash antes que Metallica), Flipper. Los «beach punks» de Los Ángeles: Germs, X, Black Flag (Damaged), Descendents, Gun Club (Fire Of Love), Bad Religion. El jazz-core de Minutemen y Saccharine Trust; en el Medio Oeste, Husker Du y Replacements cambian el hardcore para siempre; en Chicago, Naked Raygun y Big Black de Steve Albini; en Europa, The Ex y los italianos CCCP.
scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

podcast.title: Evolution from Jazz Fusion (1976)
podcast.body: The band originally started as a jazz fusion band in 1976 before shifting towards a harder, louder, and faster sound, drawing inspiration from Black Sabbath and early punk rock. "They started out as a jazz fusion band in 1976, but they were also interested in groups like Black Sabbath and some of the punk rock that was starting to come out of New York and the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: All-Black Punk Band
podcast.body: The novelty of an all-black band playing punk rock, a genre often perceived as predominantly white, was a notable aspect of Bad Brains' presence. "But then there was this novelty of seeing an all-black band playing punk rock, which was supposedly a very white thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dave Grohl's All-Time Favorite
podcast.body: The Bad Brains are identified as a legendary DC band and one of Dave Grohl's all-time favorites. Their influence is evident as they appeared as guest musicians on the Foo Fighters' song "Feast or Famine," recorded near Grohl's childhood home in Arlington, Virginia. "Dave Grohl had to have this legendary DC band in one of his all-time favorites on at least one song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Formation as Mindpower
podcast.body: The band initially started as a jazz fusion group named Mindpower before transitioning to a faster and harder musical style. "They started as a jazz fusion group known as Mindpower, but the more they played, the faster and harder the music got."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation in Washington D.C.
podcast.body: As the Detroit band Death was breaking up, Bad Brains began to form in Washington D.C., becoming a seminal group in the hardcore punk scene. "Just as Death was breaking up in Detroit, bad brains was coming together in Washington, DC."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foundation for American Hardcore
podcast.body: Bad Brains was profoundly influential, credited with laying some of the fundamental groundwork for all American hardcore music that emerged in the 1980s. "bad brains was so influential that they can be credited with laying down some of the foundations for all the American hardcore that was to come in the 1980s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Funk Basslines in Early Alt-Rock
podcast.body: The Bad Brains are listed as an example of an early punk rock band whose bass lines incorporated "funk sounds," illustrating how these elements were part of alt-rock from its inception and paved the way for rap and hip hop integration. "Just go back and listen to the bass lines of songs from bands like The Slits or Publicly Wage Limited, Gang of Four, The Bad Brains, Early Red Hot Chili Peppers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Genre Blending
podcast.body: Inspired by Bob Marley, Bad Brains incorporated reggae into their sound, introducing the genre to a new generation of kids. They later expanded their sound further by integrating funk, soul, and even hip hop. "And because they were big Bob Marley fans, they also eventually incorporated reggae into their sound, bringing that genre to a whole new generation of kids."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Genre Blending and Influence
podcast.body: Being big Bob Marley fans, Bad Brains eventually incorporated Reggae into their sound, exposing the genre to a new generation of kids. Later, they further diversified their music by introducing elements of funk, soul, and even hip hop, making them hugely important on multiple levels. "And because they were big Bob Marley fans, they also eventually incorporated Reggae into their sound, bringing that genre to a whole new generation of kids. Later, funk and soul and even hip hop was introduced. Again, hugely important on so many levels."

podcast.title: Hardcore Punk Pioneers
podcast.body: Bad Brains is widely regarded as one of the pioneers of the entire hardcore punk scene, influencing the genre's development. "the bad brains is considered to be one of the pioneers of that entire scene."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Major Artists
podcast.body: Bad Brains were tremendously influential to punk kids in the DC area, including a young Dave Grohl, who was "completely besotted with them." They also influenced the Beastie Boys, Red Hot Chili Peppers, No Doubt, and even Guns N' Roses. "And that included a young Dave Grohl, who became completely besotted with him. So with the Beastie boys and the Chili Peppers and no doubt, and even Guns and Roses, that Bad Brains were great."

"Tremendously influential to punk kids in the DC area. And that included a young Dave Grohl, who became completely besotted with him."

podcast.title: Influence on Seattle Scene
podcast.body: Tracks from Bad Brains were featured on homemade punk cassettes distributed by Buzz Osborne in Aberdeen, Washington, influencing the developing Seattle rock scene. "Buzz Osborne began giving out cassettes featuring his favorite punk songs, All Indie bands, TBI from the stuages, tracks from bad brains and black flag, and Buzz gave these tapes only to people he considered cool."

podcast.title: Initial Band Name and Genre Shift
podcast.body: Bad Brains originally started as a jazz fusion group named "Mind Power." As they continued to play, their music became progressively faster and harder, leading them to change their name, inspired by the Ramones' song "Bad Brain," and embrace hardcore. "They started as a jazz fusion group known as Mindpower, but the more they played, the faster and harder the music got. And that's when they changed their name, inspired by the Ramonesong, Bad Brain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Versatility
podcast.body: Although known for their hard, loud, and fast music, Bad Brains also incorporated reggae and funk into their sound whenever it suited their mood. "Although the band would veer into reggae and funk whenever the mood suited them."

podcast.title: Name Inspiration
podcast.body: They changed their name to Bad Brains, inspired by a Ramones song titled "Bad Brain." "And that's when they changed their name, inspired by the Ramonesong, Bad Brain."

podcast.title: Name Inspired by Ramones Song
podcast.body: The band changed their name to Bad Brains, taking inspiration from a song by The Ramones also titled "Bad Brain." "They changed their name to Bad Brains after the Ramones song Bad Brain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin of "Mosh" Term (Jamaican Accent)
podcast.body: Bad Brains, a D.C.-area band known for blending hardcore with dub and reggae, played a key role in the term "mosh" becoming prevalent. Their singer, HR, frequently encouraged audiences to "mash it up" from the stage. Due to his Jamaican accent, "mash" often came out sounding like "mosh," leading to the pronunciation shift. "HR had a Jamaican accent. So whenever he said and sang mash, it kind of came out as Mosh."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Performance During CBGB's Final Weeks
podcast.body: Bad Brains was one of the bands that performed at CBGB during its final weeks leading up to its closure in October 2006. "The final weeks featured bands like Bad Brains, The Dictators, and even Blondie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Promotion of Racial Harmony in Hardcore
podcast.body: Their presence and influence contributed to fostering rules of racial harmony within many parts of the hardcore scene. "And because of bad brains, there were rules of racial harmony in many areas of the hardcore scene."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Racial and Religious Identity
podcast.body: Every member of Bad Brains was African American and identified as Rastafarians, a distinctive feature for a hardcore band. "Another thing, every member of Bad Brains was African American. They were all Rastafarians too."

podcast.body: All members of Bad Brains were African American and Rastafarians, a unique aspect for the hardcore scene at the time. "Another thing, every member of bad brains was African American. They were all Rastafarians too."

podcast.title: Role in "Mosh" Terminology Origin
podcast.body: The DC band Bad Brains initially encouraged their fans to "mash" during shows, a term derived from the Jamaican phrase "mash it up." This term later mutated into "mosh" because the band's senior HR (likely referring to singer H.R.) had a Jamaican accent and pronounced "mash" as "mosh." "The originally encouraged fans to mash, which is their word, derived from the Jamaican phrase, mash it up against each other during their shows."

xref.body: A young musician from Aberdeen, Washington, Buzz Osborne was known for distributing homemade cassettes featuring his favorite punk songs, including tracks from indie bands, The Stooges, Bad Brains, and Black Flag, only to people he deemed "cool."
